analysis.one_liner: Suspends common bee-killing neonicotinoid pesticides until safety studies clear them.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 46 House Democrats, never got a hearing or a vote and died in the Agriculture Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ordered the EPA to suspend five neonicotinoid insecticides — chemicals used to coat seeds and treat soil and plants — on bee-attractive crops until scientific field studies show they won't harm bees, birds, and other pollinators. It would also block new registrations of these pesticides in the meantime and require the Interior Department to track native bee health and report to Congress each year. It was introduced in June 2017 and referred to the House Agriculture Committee, which never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Beekeepers and farmers who depend on bees to pollinate crops like almonds, apples, and cranberries would benefit from healthier bee populations, as would everyone who eats food that relies on pollination. Native bees, birds, and other wildlife would be protected from a pesticide class linked to mass bee deaths. Consumers get a more secure food supply; one in three bites of food in North America depends on bee pollination.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Beekeepers, pollinator-dependent farmers, and the food supply

how_it_helps.text: The bill would suspend imidacloprid, clothianidin, thiamethoxam, dinotafuran, and related nitro-group neonicotinoids on bee-attractive plants, trees, and cereals within 180 days, pending a peer-reviewed evidence evaluation and a completed field study covering chronic low-dose and cumulative exposures.

The bill's findings cite a federal survey showing 45.2% annual honeybee hive mortality in 2012-2013, record colony collapse incidents, and declines in more than 40 federally listed pollinator species, framing the bill as protection for a pollination service worth $24 billion a year to the U.S. economy.
The Interior Department would have to regularly monitor native bee populations, investigate unusual die-offs, and publish an annual public report on pollinator health.

The bill's findings cite an EPA assessment that neonicotinoid seed coatings provide little benefit to soybean yields and that the coatings are unnecessary in roughly 80 to 90 percent of row-crop uses, suggesting much of the ban would remove little productive value.

analysis.who_pays: Pesticide manufacturers that sell neonicotinoids would lose sales on seed treatments, soil applications, and foliar sprays for bee-attractive crops. Some farmers would lose a cheap, routine pest-control tool and might pay more or switch to other insecticides until the EPA completes its safety reviews. Costs of completing new field studies fall on regulators and registrants.
analysis.who_pays_short: Neonicotinoid pesticide makers and some row-crop farmers

drawbacks.text: The suspension is mandatory and near-immediate (within 180 days), before the science review it requires is finished — critics could fairly object that the bill reverses the usual EPA process, under which a pesticide stays on the market until regulators prove harm.

Farmers who rely on neonicotinoid seed treatments to protect corn, soy, and other crops from pests would lose an effective tool for those uses where the treatments do provide yield protection, and the bill offers no transition assistance or alternative pest-management funding.

If bees rebounded or the pesticides proved safe, the restriction would still have imposed compliance costs and constrained chemical options, and the required federal field studies and annual monitoring would cost taxpayer money.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stakes are large and asymmetric: pollination underpins roughly a third of North American food production, and the bill's own findings say current bee losses are too high to guarantee future pollination supply. The bill's main cost falls on pesticide makers and farmers who would need substitutes, but its findings also cite EPA's own assessment that most seed-coating uses add little yield benefit. Its genuine design weakness is that it suspends the chemicals before the studies it demands are complete, an aggressive sequencing choice an honest supporter would acknowledge.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee, then to a subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 23, 2017, with Conyers as sponsor and 25 original cosponsors, and was referred the same day to the House Committee on Agriculture.
On July 11, 2017, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Biotechnology, Horticulture, and Research, where it stayed; the action history shows no further activity.
All 46 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, without the bill receiving a hearing or floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers of neonicotinoid pesticides and the row-crop operations that depend on them are better off, since their products stayed on the market without restriction. Beekeepers and pollinator-dependent farmers gained nothing, and the bee losses the bill documented continued unaddressed by any federal statute.

for.name: John Conyers, Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Saving America's Pollinators Act and recruited 25 original cosponsors.

for.name: 45 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee
against.role: Committee of referral under Chairman K. Michael Conaway (R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup on the bill; it was sent to a subcommittee and died there.

sides.party_line_note: All 46 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; the bill was referred to a Republican-run Agriculture Committee that took no action on it.

industries.industry: Neonicotinoid pesticide manufacturers (makers of imidacloprid, clothianidin, thiamethoxam, dinotefuran)
industries.note: The bill would suspend these companies' flagship products on bee-attractive crops within 180 days and block new registrations until field studies proved safety. Their loss of sales comes at the direct benefit of pollinator health, which the findings tie to a $24 billion annual pollination service.

industries.industry: Row-crop farming and seed-treatment agriculture (corn, soy, cereals)
industries.note: Farmers would lose a cheap, standard seed-coating pesticide on bee-attractive crops, though the bill's findings cite EPA research that neonic coatings add little to soybean yields and are unneeded in 80-90% of row-crop uses.

industries.industry: Beekeepers and pollination-dependent growers (almonds, apples, cranberries, avocados)
industries.note: Healthier bee populations mean fewer colony losses for beekeepers and more reliable pollination for fruit and nut growers — and for the food supply generally.
